description:
The police can search your car without a warrant - and they've been able to for a hundred years. But there is one place that century-old power still cannot reach.

This episode explains the Fourth Amendment 'automobile exception': where it came from, what actually lets an officer open your trunk, glovebox, and the bags inside your car (probable cause, not a hunch), how far that search can go, and the bright line the Supreme Court drew in 2018 - the ground pressed against your home.

We trace the rule from a Prohibition bootlegger stopped on a Michigan highway in 1925 to a motorcycle hidden under a tarp in a Virginia driveway, and lay out the plain-English map of your rights on the road.

This is an educational documentary about settled law, presented neutrally - neither pro- nor anti-police. It is general legal education, not legal advice, and does not describe the practice of any specific jurisdiction. Some rules (such as whether the smell of marijuana alone counts as probable cause) are unsettled and vary by state.

Visual note: this video uses AI-generated symbolic reconstructions and motion graphics. They are illustrations, not authentic footage, and no real-person likeness is intended.

pinned_comment: The automobile exception is broad - broader than most people think - but it isn't infinite. It stops at the curtilage, the ground pressed against your home. Were you taught police need a warrant to search your car?
